title: Refrain: 'I am listening to Istanbul, my eyes closed'
short: Each stanza opens and closes with the same line, so the poem becomes a catalogue of sounds framed by a single act of blind listening.
body: The refrain is the poem's frame: the city is not seen but heard, and the closed eyes turn description into memory and imagination. Each stanza begins and ends with the line, except the last, which breaks the pattern. The device is a return to song-like repetition after the stark free verse of Garip (1941); by Vazgeçemediğim (1945) Orhan Veli had softened some Garip positions, objecting not to metre and rhyme as such but to treating them as essential to poetry. The poem became one of the best-known Turkish poems about Istanbul and gave its title to Talât Sait Halman's English selection of Orhan Veli (1971).

sources.cite: Yılmaz Daşcıoğlu, 'Kanık, Orhan Veli', TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi, Ek-2 (2019)

title: Sucular (water-sellers) and their bells
short: Street water-sellers announced themselves with small bells; their endless ringing far off is a sound of old Istanbul.
body: Before piped water reached all districts, sucular (water-sellers) carried water through the streets in containers on their backs or on carts and rang a bell (çıngırak) to call customers. The sound is placed 'far, very far away', as if from the past. Orhan Veli wrote a separate poem on the figure, 'Sucunun Türküsü', also held in this archive. The image places the poem in a city of trades and street life rather than of monuments.

sources.cite: Türk Dil Kurumu, Güncel Türkçe Sözlük
Talât S. Halman, A Millennium of Turkish Literature, ed. Jayne L. Warner (Syracuse University Press, 2011)

title: dalyan (fishing weir)
short: Nets are being drawn in at the dalyans, the fixed fishing weirs of stakes and nets once common along the Bosphorus.
body: A dalyan is a fixed fishery: a structure of poles and nets set in the water to catch migrating fish, with a lookout who signals when to haul. Bosphorus fishing weirs were a feature of the strait into the twentieth century. The line moves from the sky (flocks of birds 'crying, crying') to the water, and the Turkish doubled adverbs 'sürü sürü, çığlık çığlık' (in flocks, in cries) imitate the noise. Fishing, like the water-sellers, connects the listening speaker with working Istanbul.

sources.cite: Türk Dil Kurumu, Güncel Türkçe Sözlük
James W. Redhouse, A Turkish and English Lexicon (Constantinople, 1890)

title: 'A woman's feet touch the water'
short: A single erotic, quiet image among the noises: a woman's feet touching the water, perhaps from a boat or a waterside step.
body: The line is remarkable because it is not a sound at all, or only the faintest one; it is something the listening speaker imagines or remembers. It introduces the figure of a woman who returns in the fifth and sixth stanzas and finally merges with the city addressed as 'you'. The plain syntax (subject, object, verb) is typical of Orhan Veli's refusal of ornament, yet the image is sensuous and delicate.

sources.cite: Yılmaz Daşcıoğlu, 'Kanık, Orhan Veli', TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi, Ek-2 (2019)
Talât Sait Halman (trans. and intro.), I Am Listening to Istanbul: Selected Poems of Orhan Veli Kanık (New York: Corinth Books, 1971)

title: Kapalı Çarşı (the Covered Bazaar)
short: The Grand Bazaar, a vast roofed market begun in the fifteenth century, is 'cool, cool' in its shaded streets.
body: Kapalı Çarşı, the 'Covered Market' or Grand Bazaar, grew from Mehmed II's bedesten after the conquest of 1453 into a covered city of streets, shops and inns. Its stone vaults keep it cool: hence 'serin serin'. Orhan Veli also wrote a poem titled 'Kapalı Çarşı' (also held in this archive). The stanza lists sensations rather than sights: coolness, chirping, pigeons, hammers, the smell of sweat; the doubled adjectives (serin serin, cıvıl cıvıl) are a feature of spoken Turkish.

sources.cite: Talât S. Halman, A Millennium of Turkish Literature, ed. Jayne L. Warner (Syracuse University Press, 2011)
Türk Dil Kurumu, Güncel Türkçe Sözlük

title: Mahmutpaşa
short: The busy market quarter running down from the Grand Bazaar towards Eminönü, named after the fifteenth-century grand vizier Mahmud Pasha.
body: Mahmutpaşa is the steep commercial district between the Grand Bazaar and the Golden Horn at Eminönü, named after Mahmud Pasha Angelović, grand vizier to Mehmed II, whose mosque and baths stand there. It is a quarter of crowded shops and cheap goods, and 'cıvıl cıvıl' (chirping, bustling, full of lively noise) catches its crowds. With the pigeon-filled courtyards of the next line, which suggest the mosque yards of the old city, the stanza moves through the historic peninsula.

sources.cite: Talât S. Halman, A Millennium of Turkish Literature, ed. Jayne L. Warner (Syracuse University Press, 2011)
Türk Dil Kurumu, Güncel Türkçe Sözlük

title: Hammers from the docks
short: The sound of hammering from the docks brings the industrial, labouring city into the spring air.
body: The docks (doklar, from English 'dock' via French) of the Golden Horn and the shipyards at Kasımpaşa and Hasköy were places of shipbuilding and repair. The hammers and 'smells of sweat on the lovely spring wind' join work and pleasure, the ugly and the beautiful, in the same breath; this refusal to separate 'poetic' from 'unpoetic' material is central to Orhan Veli's practice and to the Garip preface's attack on special poetic diction.

title: âlem (world; a drinking party)
short: 'The intoxication of old revels': in colloquial Turkish an âlem is a night of drinking and merriment as well as a 'world'.
body: Âlem is the Arabic ʿālam, 'world', but in everyday Istanbul Turkish it also means a party or night out, a spree, especially with drink and music ('âlem yapmak'). 'Eski âlemlerin sarhoşluğu' is therefore both 'the drunkenness of past worlds' and 'the hangover of old revels', and the ambiguity suits a stanza of nostalgia for a vanished city. Ahmet Haşim, earlier in this archive, uses âlem in the grand sense ('Âlemlerimizden'); Orhan Veli uses it in the tavern sense.

sources.cite: Türk Dil Kurumu, Güncel Türkçe Sözlük
James W. Redhouse, A Turkish and English Lexicon (Constantinople, 1890)

title: yalı, kayıkhane (waterside mansion; boathouse)
short: A yalı is a wooden waterside mansion on the Bosphorus; its dim boathouses open directly onto the sea.
body: Yalı comes from Greek gialos, 'shore', and names the waterfront houses, often of wood, built by Ottoman officials and wealthy families along the Bosphorus. Kayıkhane joins Turkish kayık (rowing boat) and Persian khāna (house): the boathouse on the ground floor where caiques were kept. Orhan Veli himself was born in Beykoz on the Bosphorus. The 'dim' boathouses of a yalı are an image of old, fading elegance, set beside the memory of old revels.

sources.cite: Sevan Nişanyan, Nişanyan Sözlük: Çağdaş Türkçenin Etimolojisi (online)

title: lodos (the south-west wind)
short: The lodos is the warm south-westerly that brings storms to Istanbul; here its roar has died away.
body: Lodos is the south-west wind of the Marmara region, notorious in Istanbul for high seas, rain and damaged boats and for a heavy, restless mood. The paradox 'the roar of lodos winds that have died down' is the sound of an absence, heard only in memory, like the 'old revels' above. The stanza is the shortest in the poem (five lines), and its sound-words (uğultu, the roaring hum) give way directly to the refrain.

sources.cite: Türk Dil Kurumu, Güncel Türkçe Sözlük

title: yosma (a pretty, flirtatious woman)
short: A yosma is a coquettish, attractive woman; men's swearing, songs and catcalls follow her along the pavement.
body: Yosma is a colloquial word for a pretty, flirtatious woman, often with a hint of the street; it is common in folk songs. The line that follows is a list of crowd sounds: 'küfürler, şarkılar, türküler, lâf atmalar' (curses, songs, folk songs, catcalls), lâf atmak being the remarks men throw at a passing woman. The tone is unsentimental and urban. Then something falls from her hand, and the speaker, eyes still closed, guesses: 'it must be a rose'.

sources.cite: Türk Dil Kurumu, Güncel Türkçe Sözlük
James W. Redhouse, A Turkish and English Lexicon (Constantinople, 1890)

title: 'It must be a rose'
short: The guessed rose is the only conventional poetic flower in the poem, and it arrives as a supposition.
body: Orhan Veli's Garip preface had attacked the stock apparatus of poetry; the rose, emblem of the beloved in divan verse, is the most traditional poetic object of all. Here it appears only as a guess by a man who cannot see: 'it must be a rose'. The line can be read as gentle irony, the poet catching himself in a poetic cliché, or as a sincere tenderness that the earlier list of curses and catcalls makes more touching. Either way, the rose leads into the final stanza's address to a beloved.

sources.cite: Orhan Veli, Oktay Rifat, Melih Cevdet, Garip (Istanbul, 1941), Orhan Veli's preface ('Garip' önsözü)

anchor: Alnın sıcak mı değil mi, biliyorum
title: The shift to 'you'
short: In the last stanza the speaker suddenly addresses 'you': your forehead, your lips, your heartbeat. Is the beloved a woman, or Istanbul itself?
body: Up to this point the poem has listed the city's sounds in the third person. In the last stanza a bird flutters 'in your skirts', and the speaker says he knows whether your forehead is hot and your lips wet, and understands from your heartbeat. The 'you' may be the woman of the previous stanzas, now held close, or it may be Istanbul personified as a beloved whose body he knows by touch and pulse. Most readers take the ambiguity to be deliberate: the city and the loved woman merge, so that listening to Istanbul becomes an act of love. The repeated 'biliyorum' (I know) replaces the earlier uncertainty of 'olmalı' (must be).

sources.cite: Talât Sait Halman (trans. and intro.), I Am Listening to Istanbul: Selected Poems of Orhan Veli Kanık (New York: Corinth Books, 1971)
Yılmaz Daşcıoğlu, 'Kanık, Orhan Veli', TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi, Ek-2 (2019)

title: fıstık (stone pine)
short: 'A white moon rises from behind the pines': fıstık here means the umbrella-shaped stone pines (fıstık çamı) of the Bosphorus hills.
body: Fıstık normally means a nut (pistachio or pine nut), but 'fıstık çamı', the stone pine with its flat umbrella crown, is a characteristic tree of Istanbul's hills and old gardens, and 'fıstıklar' is a natural shortening. The rising white moon is the poem's only full visual image, yet it is still known through the heartbeat of the beloved in the next line. Night falls over the city as the poem closes.

sources.cite: Türk Dil Kurumu, Güncel Türkçe Sözlük

title: The broken refrain
short: The final refrain drops 'gözlerim kapalı': the poem ends on simple listening, as if the eyes have opened or the frame has dissolved.
body: Every stanza until now has closed with the full refrain. The final line shortens it to 'İstanbul'u dinliyorum.' and ends with a full stop. The change is small but deliberate. It can suggest that the act of imagination is complete and the city now present, or that the beloved's heartbeat has replaced the blind listening. Such quiet variation of a fixed refrain is a device of song, and the poem's popularity owes much to this musical shape.
